paper.title: Acorus tatarinowii and its bioactive constituents: Ethnopharmacology, chemical variability, preclinical pharmacology, safety, and translational challenges.
paper.abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Acorus tatarinowii Schott. has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine for disorders associated with impaired consciousness, cognitive dysfunction, epilepsy, and gastrointestinal disturbance. Modern studies have explored related pharmacological activities, but marked preparation-dependent chemical variability and safety concerns surrounding α-asarone and β-asarone complicate interpretation and translation.
AIM OF THE STUDY: This narrative review critically integrates the ethnopharmacological uses, phytochemistry, preclinical pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, toxicology, and regulatory evidence of Acorus tatarinowii and its bioactive constituents.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection were searched for relevant literature published from January 1, 2010 to May 1, 2026. Earlier foundational studies and regulatory documents were additionally considered when relevant to traditional use, pharmacokinetics, toxicology, carcinogenicity, or regulatory assessment.
RESULTS: More than 160 constituents have been identified, with α-asarone and β-asarone being the most extensively studied. Volatile oils, aqueous and alcoholic extracts, purified fractions, and isolated compounds differ substantially in composition and should not be regarded as interchangeable. Preclinical studies report neurological, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, anti-inflammatory, and other activities associated with neuronal excitability, oxidative stress, inflammation, autophagy, mitochondrial function, and barrier integrity. However, most mechanistic evidence remains associative, direct causal validation is limited, and constituent interactions are poorly defined. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate rapid absorption and brain distribution of asarone isomers, whereas toxicological evidence raises concerns regarding dose-dependent central effects, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, and reproductive and developmental toxicity.
CONCLUSION: Acorus tatarinowii exhibits diverse preclinical pharmacological activities, but clinical efficacy, a validated therapeutic window, and long-term safety remain unestablished. Future translation requires authenticated and chemically standardized preparations, quantitative control of asarone isomers, integrated exposure-response assessment, direct mechanistic validation, and rigorous long-term safety evaluation.

paper.title: Toward optimised magnetic seizure therapy for depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis of stimulation parameters and clinical outcomes.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) is a seizure-based neuromodulation treatment for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) that aims to combine antidepressant efficacy with better cognitive tolerability than electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). However, associations between stimulation parameters and clinical outcomes remain unclear.
METHODS: We systematically reviewed clinical MST studies identified through PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL. Study characteristics, stimulation parameters, antidepressant and cognitive outcomes, suicidality, and safety data were extracted. Descriptive synthesis, exploratory descriptive comparisons, and random-effects meta-analyses of response and remission rates were performed where possible.
RESULTS: Twenty-three reports representing 19 independent cohorts met inclusion criteria. The pooled proportions of antidepressant response and remission following MST were 52.4% and 30.6%, respectively, reflecting outcomes in MST-treated groups rather than comparative efficacy estimates. Across studies, cognitive tolerability was generally favourable, with an acceptable safety profile. Early studies varied substantially in stimulation frequency, pulse number, stimulation duration, dosing strategy, and treatment course. Contemporary protocols increasingly converged on high-frequency stimulation (predominantly 100 Hz), approximately 1000 pulses per train, stimulation durations of about 10 s, and seizure-threshold-guided dosing. Nevertheless, response and remission rates remained variable. Both vertex and frontal stimulation were associated with positive outcomes, but the independent contribution of coil placement could not be determined because stimulation parameters substantially co-varied.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates clinically relevant antidepressant outcomes following MST, while a large randomised trial in major depressive disorder demonstrated non-inferior antidepressant efficacy compared with ECT and reported more favourable cognitive tolerability. Contemporary protocols increasingly converge across several stimulation parameters, while uncertainty remains regarding characteristics that still vary across studies. Coil placement remains an important unresolved methodological factor. Future controlled studies should compare stimulation targets under otherwise standardised treatment conditions to optimise MST protocols.

paper.title: Intraoperative electrocorticography in epilepsy surgery: background, technological advances, clinical impact, and current recommendations - a literature review.
paper.abstract: Epilepsy surgery has evolved through technological innovation and refined therapeutic strategies, aiming to achieve accurate resection of the epileptogenic cortex while minimizing neurological morbidity. Intraoperative electrocorticography (ioECoG) remains an important adjunct for intraoperative electrophysiological assessment and real-time cortical monitoring. Advances such as high-density electrode arrays and extended recording protocols have significantly improved spatial and temporal resolution, enhancing surgical precision and decision-making. A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, SciELO, and LILACS to identify clinically relevant publications addressing the role of intraoperative electrocorticography in epilepsy surgery. Representative studies published between 2000 and 2025 were selected according to their relevance to surgical decision-making, anesthetic considerations, electrophysiological biomarkers, and postoperative seizure outcomes in adult and pediatric populations. ioECoG has progressed from conventional subdural recordings to high-resolution multichannel systems integrated with neuroimaging and computational analysis. This evolution allows precise delineation of epileptogenic and irritative zones, improved electroclinical correlation, and individualized surgical strategies. Electrophysiological biomarkers, particularly high-frequency oscillations (HFOs) and fast ripples (FRs), have strengthened its predictive capacity. Several studies have reported improved seizure freedom rates associated with ioECoG-guided resections, particularly when complete elimination of epileptiform activity is achieved. High-density systems and HFO/FR analysis enable safer, more targeted resections. Integration with advanced neuroimaging and standardized multimodal protocols has consolidated ioECoG as an important adjunctive tool of contemporary epilepsy surgery.

paper.title: Rodent studies of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy-induced neonatal seizures: A systematic review on model variations and reporting standards.
paper.abstract: Neonatal seizures resulting from hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) are common and associated with long-term neurological impairment and developmental delays. This clinical burden necessitates better understanding of underlying mechanisms to improve treatment strategies. Rodent models are essential to this field and extensively investigated. However, translating these findings to human patients remains challenging. This review evaluates all preclinical research on rodent models of HIE-induced neonatal seizures to date, assessing model variations, methodological quality, and translational potential. We conducted a systematic search in PubMed and Embase up to March 10, 2025, identifying 134 publications describing 186 HIE induction protocols. Studies exposing rodents to hypoxia at or before postnatal day 21 and presenting unique data on seizure occurrence were included. Results were synthesized narratively. Identified induction protocols comprised three model types: (1) ambient hypoxia, (2) surgically induced ischemia, and (3) ambient hypoxia combined with ischemia. Rat models were most frequently used (67%), and the most common method of HIE induction was ambient hypoxia (63%). Seizures were reported in 88% of model variations, but detection methods, definitions, and monitoring timing varied widely, limiting comparability of seizure outcome data. Potential links between lower age at induction and increased seizure susceptibility and between the combined use of hypoxic/hypercapnic conditions and increased seizure occurrence were observed. Antiseizure medications were inconsistently investigated; phenobarbital showed variable, age-dependent efficacy. Risk of bias, assessed using SYRCLE's risk of bias tool, was generally high. Altogether, this systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of rodent models of HIE-induced neonatal seizures. Although these models have advanced understanding in this field, variability in model design and incomplete reporting limit objective identification of a gold standard model with optimal translatability. Standardization of model parameters, detailed monitoring of behavioral and electrophysiological seizure characteristics, and rigorous reporting practices will enhance reproducibility, optimize laboratory animal use, and strengthen clinical relevance of preclinical findings.

paper.title: Gene therapy for developmental and epileptic encephalopathies: a mechanism-driven framework for therapeutic design.
paper.abstract: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of severe neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by early-onset seizures, developmental delay or regression, and cognitive impairment. Many DEEs arise from genetic variants that disrupt neuronal excitability, synaptic function, metabolism, cell signaling, or epigenetic regulation. As the genetic architecture of DEEs has expanded, genetic therapy has emerged as a promising strategy to address their underlying molecular causes. Preclinical studies using adeno-associated viral vectors, antisense oligonucleotides, RNA-based therapies, and CRISPR-derived approaches have shown that early intervention can reduce seizure burden, improve neurological phenotypes, and extend survival in selected models. These advances also highlight the importance of therapeutic timing, cell-type specificity, and appropriate vector design. In this Review, we adopt a mechanism-centered framework that links major biological classes of DEEs to gene therapy design parameters, including modality, vector, promoter, and developmental timing, while also considering translational challenges and future directions for precision medicine in this field.
